attacks.claim: The rollback path re-imports only new Ghost signups into MailPoet. Unsubscribes, bounces, and complaints recorded in Ghost after cutover are not written back, so a rollback after the first Ghost send can re-mail people who opted out. This breaks the plan's own suppression guarantee, and a sent email cannot be recalled.
attacks.evidence: rollback = repoint DNS and re-enable MailPoet sending, with any new Ghost signups exported and re-imported to MailPoet

attacks.claim: No delta sync or write freeze is defined between the production import and DNS cutover. MailPoet changes made in that window, including unsubscribes from the week-3 Thursday send, would be missing or stale in Ghost, and Ghost could then mail opted-out readers. The production import is also not placed in the timeline, and the plan has two systems that could both be authoritative during the overlap.
attacks.evidence: counts reconciled against MailPoet totals ... before the production import; Week 3: final Thursday send on MailPoet; Week 4: cutover Tuesday; ABSENT: production import step in Section 7

attacks.claim: Paid-member state is outside the rollback. Stripe subscriptions and webhooks point at Ghost after cutover, and the plan never says how webhook endpoints, subscription status, or membership-plugin records would be restored or reconciled if rollback is triggered.
attacks.evidence: Stripe: existing Stripe account connected directly; no change in processor. ABSENT: webhook repointing or reversal, and handling for Ghost-created paid members

attacks.claim: The first send to roughly 44,000 readers is irreversible and has no defined abort. The 2-hour auto-release is conditional on metrics, but the plan names no owner who checks thresholds, no way to hold or cancel the release, and no action if thresholds are breached. The 2,000-recipient seed also gives weak statistics for a 0.1% complaint threshold, and no historical MailPoet baseline is given to anchor either threshold.
attacks.evidence: the remainder sends 2 hours later if bounce rate < 2% and complaint rate < 0.1%; ABSENT: owner, stop mechanism, breach action, baseline

attacks.claim: The Mailgun cost is a self-estimate with no quoted rate, tier, or source, yet the $300/mo constraint check depends on it. The plan also has no spend cap or billing alert, and the seed, retry, and rollback re-send paths can add message volume beyond the baseline.
attacks.evidence: Estimated $90/mo at our volume (46k x ~4.3 sends/month). ABSENT: pricing tier, per-message rate, usage cap, or billing alert

attacks.claim: Transition-period spend is unbudgeted. The old VPS runs through the build and for 30 days after cutover, the new VPS runs in parallel, and staging and scratch instances run in weeks 1-2. None of this is in the $140/mo or $95/mo comparison, so migration-window spend is understated.
attacks.evidence: WordPress stays running read-only on the old VPS for 30 days; Week 1: VPS + Ghost + backups; subscriber and content dry runs on staging

attacks.claim: The headline total is labelled as VPS cost, but the figure is VPS ($48) plus Mailgun ($90) plus unpriced storage. The label is misleading, and the storage cost is not stated, so the $140 figure cannot be checked against the cap.
attacks.evidence: Total run cost: ~$140/mo VPS + Mailgun + storage, vs $95/mo today.

attacks.claim: Consent source and IP fields have no stated mapping into Ghost's schema, and no import test shows they survive. Without this, the consent evidence the plan relies on may be dropped or stored in an unplanned place.
attacks.evidence: consent source/IP where recorded; ABSENT: field mapping or import test for consent fields

attacks.claim: The suppression safeguard against re-mailing opt-outs is asserted but not shown to work. No staging run confirms that suppressed status survives import and send in Ghost, and re-mailing an opted-out reader cannot be undone.
attacks.evidence: Unsubscribed and bounced addresses are imported as suppressed (never as active), so nobody who opted out is re-mailed. ABSENT: staging test of suppressed status through import and send

attacks.claim: Mailgun, Postmark, and the unnamed object-storage provider receive reader PII with no stated DPA, sub-processor review, data region, or transfer terms. Lawful basis for transferring consent records is also not addressed.
attacks.evidence: Mailgun only receives per-send recipient batches; nightly encrypted dumps to object storage (no provider named); ABSENT: DPA, sub-processor list, transfer review

attacks.claim: Credentials for Stripe, Mailgun, SMTP, and the Ghost Admin and Members APIs have no stated storage, scoping, rotation, or exclusion from exports and dumps. Payment and bulk-send keys are high-value.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: secrets management or rotation plan; Stripe: existing Stripe account connected directly; Mailgun

attacks.claim: Nightly encrypted dumps and weekly plaintext member CSV and JSON exports sit in object storage with no key owner, key custody, access policy, or retention limit for the exports. The exports include full subscriber and consent data.
attacks.evidence: nightly encrypted dumps to object storage (30-day retention); members CSV export and JSON content export are scheduled weekly (cron, stored with the DB dumps)

attacks.claim: Staging, the week-2 scratch Ghost, and the dry-run environments each hold a full copy of subscriber, consent, and paid-member data. The plan sets no access control, teardown date, or purge check for these copies.
attacks.evidence: Dry-run import on staging in week 1; restore one export into a scratch Ghost instance in week 2

attacks.claim: The plan defines no authentication, staff roles, MFA, or export and send permissions for the Ghost admin, even though it holds the full subscriber list and consent records for several people.
attacks.evidence: Owner: dev (0.5 FTE) + managing editor; editor training; ABSENT: roles, MFA, export and send authorization

attacks.claim: The 4 vCPU / 8 GB box is never load-tested at 46k recipients, and it runs Ghost web, sending, and MySQL together. This is the same contention pattern that caused the four prior send-day outages, and the plan has no isolation or send-window guard.
attacks.evidence: new 4 vCPU / 8 GB VPS ($48/mo ...); MySQL 8 on the same box; ABSENT: timed full-list send or load test

attacks.claim: There is no monitoring, alerting, health check, or on-call escalation for Ghost, MySQL, Mailgun, or the backup job. The plan's own success measure is zero send-day outages, but nothing detects a failure during a send.
attacks.evidence: Zero send-day outages over the first quarter.; ABSENT: monitoring, alerting, or on-call section

attacks.claim: Backups are described but not restore-tested. The only round-trip test covers the JSON and CSV exports, not the nightly encrypted MySQL dumps that are the actual recovery path, and no restore-time objective is defined.
attacks.evidence: nightly encrypted dumps to object storage (30-day retention); restore one export into a scratch Ghost instance in week 2; ABSENT: DB dump restore test

attacks.claim: The weekly export is presented as an existing Ghost capability, but no mechanism for producing it on a schedule is shown. The exit path depends on it, and nothing shows it runs unattended.
attacks.evidence: Ghost's members CSV export and JSON content export are scheduled weekly (cron, stored with the DB dumps); ABSENT: export mechanism or unattended run test

attacks.claim: The URL-preservation claim (/YYYY/MM/slug/ via routes.yaml) has no prototype or cited Ghost capability behind it. The 2,000-URL crawl gate is not yet demonstrated, so SEO and link continuity are unverified.
attacks.evidence: URL structure kept identical (/YYYY/MM/slug/) via Ghost routes.yaml; a crawl of the 2,000 most-visited URLs ... must return 200/301 before cutover

attacks.claim: The rollback is never rehearsed. Its reverse export and re-import into MailPoet has no schedule, owner, or failure handling, unlike the forward export and the Postmark exit drill, and it does not cover state changed after the first Ghost send.
attacks.evidence: rollback = repoint DNS and re-enable MailPoet sending, with any new Ghost signups exported and re-imported to MailPoet; ABSENT: rollback rehearsal

attacks.claim: The exit path is rehearsed only with a 50-address list, which does not exercise 46k-scale throughput, rate limits, or failure handling. The plan also does not say whether suppression, consent, and bounce state survive the export-to-new-sender round trip.
attacks.evidence: In week 2 we rehearse this end to end with a 50-address internal list through Postmark Broadcasts; the exit is: disable Ghost newsletter sending and load the weekly members export into another bulk sender

attacks.claim: The 37 members with mismatched emails are to be resolved by hand before cutover, with no procedure, verification step, or owner. Manual matching of payment records to accounts risks linking one person's payment data to another's account, and it gates cutover readiness.
attacks.evidence: 37 members with mismatched emails were identified in a dry run and will be resolved by hand before cutover

attacks.claim: The plan does not say how existing paying members sign in or access paywalled content on cutover day. The 37 mismatched members have no access path, so paying readers could lose access at the moment of cutover.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: member login or access flow; 37 members ... will be resolved by hand before cutover

attacks.claim: Four workstreams (host migration, email provider change, membership consolidation, and content and theme migration) are packed into 4 weeks at 0.5 FTE. There is no prioritization, descope path, or send-day coverage if the timeline slips, and the week-4 cutover has no buffer or go/no-go criteria.
attacks.evidence: Owner: dev (0.5 FTE) + managing editor | 4 weeks; Week 4: cutover Tuesday, seeded first send Thursday

attacks.claim: The old WordPress and MailPoet host stays online for 30 days, and the plan does not say whether its admin, send capability, and plugin stack are locked down or patched. Rollback depends on re-enabling sending from that host.
attacks.evidence: WordPress stays running read-only on the old VPS for 30 days; rollback = repoint DNS and re-enable MailPoet sending

attacks.claim: Sender and domain change is not announced to the 46,000 readers, and the first send comes from a new Mailgun-backed domain. Warm-up and the seed mitigate this partly, but there is no reader notice or sender-recognition step.
attacks.evidence: Mailgun domain warm-up (SPF/DKIM/DMARC); no reader notice in the artifact

attacks.claim: Success measures are internal operational metrics only. Nothing tracks reader retention, opens, or paid conversion after the move, and the theme and paywall port has no reader-facing acceptance criteria or accessibility checks for alt text or contrast.
attacks.evidence: Zero send-day outages over the first quarter.; Week 2: theme port, routes/redirects, export round-trip test

attacks.claim: Transactional mail is called provider-independent, but no transactional provider is named or configured, so the portability claim is unverified.
attacks.evidence: Transactional mail (sign-in links, receipts) goes over plain SMTP and is provider-independent.

attacks.claim: The weekly full exports and nightly dumps run on the production box with no schedule relative to send days, so they could collide with the Thursday send and the staged 2-hour release.
attacks.evidence: members CSV export and JSON content export are scheduled weekly; nightly encrypted dumps to object storage

attacks.claim: No erasure or deletion procedure covers the weekly exports and 30-day backups, and no privacy-policy or notice update is scheduled before subscriber data moves to new processors.
attacks.evidence: nightly encrypted dumps to object storage (30-day retention); ABSENT: deletion procedure and privacy-notice update
